newsitem.title: JAPAN: INSTANT VIEW - Japan Sept current account surplus.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Japan Sept current account surplus.

text.p: The following are comments from economists on Japan's current account surplus which fell 35.6 percent from a year earlier to 727.4 billion yen in September, the Ministry of Finance said on Monday.
For the six months to September, the surplus fell 35.3 percent to 3.332 trillion yen.
JASON JAMES, STRATEGIST, JAMES CAPEL, TOKYO

"They are watching the number quite closely at the moment because the yen has been moving around sharply over the last week. This should take some pressure off the dollar and perhaps allow a little bit of a rebound in the dollar."

"However, these balance of payments figures...they usually broadly reflect what we have already seen in the customs-cleared trade figures for the month. We knew the trade figures were down 30 percent year-on-year, so there is no big surprise in these figures. But it may allow some end to the rise in the yen we've seen in the last two or three days."
MIKIHIRO MATSUOKA, ECONOMIST, DAIWA INSTITUTE OF RESEARCH

"I think the pace of the reduction in the current account surplus would be affecting the foreign exchange market. We've seen export values increase since mid-1995 and the increase in imports has been flattening since the beginning of 1996."
"We could expect the pace of slowdown or reduction in the trade surplus and current account surplus to continue in the coming months."

Matsuoka added that there would be some favourable effects on exports from the weaker yen. Exports can be expected to grow both in terms of volume and value in the coming months with imports flattening out, he said.

James said he expects the current account surplus in the latter half of the fiscal year ending on March 31 to decrease 25 percent from the same period a year earlier, which should be good news for the economy.
TETSURO SAWANO, ECONOMIST, NIKKO RESEARCH CENTRE

"The drop in the current account surplus was smaller than expected in September, due to an about 1.5 times increase in the services trade deficit. However, it is clear that the decline in the merchandise trade is slowing down. So the general trend of the current account surplus is that it will continue to fall but at a milder rate."
